text:
🚨🇲🇽 <u>Sinaloa's governor lasted 34 hours back in office before quitting again</u>

Rubén Rocha Moya returned to the Sinaloa governorship after 112 days of leave — then requested indefinite leave again just 34 hours later, once Sheinbaum and Morena publicly distanced themselves. His original May 1 exit followed a US accusation naming him and 9 other officials over alleged ties to a Sinaloa cartel faction — an accusation Washington has never backed with a single charge in a Mexican court.

🇲🇽📈 <u>Mexican formal wages hit their highest level on record</u>

The average wage registered with the IMSS reached 673.9 pesos a day in July — the highest on record, up 42.4 pesos over the year, per El Economista — with 22.76 million formal jobs on the books, the most ever for a July. A seasonal dip in headcount, driven by the end of the school year and the harvest cycle, didn't touch the wage floor that keeps climbing under the 4T.

⚖️🇲🇽 <u>The governor in charge when the 43 vanished is now in a maximum-security cell</u>

Ángel Aguirre Rivero — governor of Guerrero the night the 43 Ayotzinapa students were forcibly disappeared in 2014 — has been arrested by the FGR and sent to the Altiplano maximum-security prison, accused of forced disappearance and of ordering the destruction of evidence in the hours after Iguala. Eleven years on, the reopened case is finally reaching the officials who ran the state, not just the foot soldiers.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Why Alito won't let go of the PRI</u>

Contralínea lays out the math behind Alejandro "Alito" Moreno's grip on the PRI: 800 million pesos a year in public financing from the INE, which he now controls after rewriting the party statutes to keep himself leader until 2032 — all while facing two desafuero requests, an 83.5-million-peso embezzlement case from his time as governor of Campeche, and real estate quietly parked in Texas. The party is polling toward extinction; the bag of public money is the only thing worth staying for.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>The CIA saw Salinas coming — and liked what it saw</u>

Declassified CIA files show US intelligence had Carlos Salinas de Gortari pegged years before 1988 as an "ambitious technocrat" with Harvard credentials and "strong presidential ambitions" — and flatly acknowledged the stolen election that made him president, noting "a massive fraud without doubt would have produced a clearer result." The architect of Mexico's fire-sale privatizations was Washington's kind of president, and Washington knew it from the start.

🇲🇽🏛️ <u>INAH unearths a lost civilization in Veracruz</u>

Archaeologists in Coatepec, Veracruz have uncovered a 1,400-year-old ceremonial platform and a 1.88-meter stone stela carved with rulers receiving a sacred fluid from a deity — iconography with Maya echoes but belonging to no known culture, ruled out as Totonac. Sheinbaum called the find "very relevant" and pledged federal funds for its research and restoration. Mexico keeps digging up proof that its history runs deeper than any empire that came after.

🇲🇽📜 <u>Mexico opens its second-largest archive — to guard the memory of the land</u>

Sheinbaum inaugurated Mexico's new Archivo General Agrario in the historic center of the capital — the second most important archive in the country after the AGN, holding 171 million documents across 45,000 linear meters, including every land-restitution decree for the 60,000+ hectares returned to campesinos since the 4T began. Land reform, filed in fireproof vaults. The record of who the land belongs to isn't going anywhere.

🇲🇽🐉 Mexico defends its own producers — on its own terms

On Aug. 15, Mexico imposed a definitive anti-dumping duty of $0.1488 per kilogram on Chinese ammonium sulfate fertilizer. When reporters tried to frame it as payback for Beijing's new tariffs of up to 51.6% on Mexican pecans, President Sheinbaum shut it down: "It's about a different matter. It's not political."

The detail that matters: this investigation opened in February 2025 — long before the current US pressure campaign and before the pecan dispute even existed. This is Mexico using the same trade-defense tools every serious economy uses: not as a US proxy, not as a China supplicant, but as a state protecting its own farmers and industry on the merits.

That's what multipolarity actually looks like. Mexico can duty Chinese fertilizer, contest China's pecan tariffs, sign with the EU, and prepare for APEC in Beijing — all at once. Diversification means never having to ask permission. One partner threatens tariffs; sovereignty means you always have somewhere else to turn.

🇲🇽🔥 Trump wants a "much better deal" — Mexico says it's already writing its own

On Aug. 21, Trump told reporters Washington is drawing up a "new" trade deal with Mexico, one he promised would be "much better for the United States." Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard's reply was telling: Mexico is on "its own path," not racing Canada, and expects an outcome shaped by its own interests — not dictated from the north.

The real story is the myth Ebrard dismantled. Washington keeps casting Mexico as China's "back door" into the US market. Mexico's Economy Ministry says the numbers refuse to cooperate: alleged Chinese transshipment through Mexico is barely 1% of Mexican exports — while the US imports far more directly from China than ever moves through Mexico. The empire manufactures a threat, then bills Mexico to solve it.

Sovereignty isn't defiance — it's arithmetic. With the EU deal signed, USMCA under review, and APEC in Beijing this November, Mexico keeps every door open and refuses to be scapegoated for a trade war it didn't start.

🇲🇽⚖️ 23 governors close ranks with Sheinbaum: "Outside the law, nothing — above the law, no one." Mexico's 23 Morena governors and the Head of Government of Mexico City signed a joint statement backing the President and calling Sinaloa governor Rubén Rocha Moya to "maturity and responsibility" after he retook his post. "No individual decision can stand above the collective project or the citizens' mandate," they wrote. "She leads the destiny of the nation with legitimacy, honesty and leadership." The movement is bigger than any one official.
